title: ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi
description: An introduction to ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi, the Hawaiian language, covering pronunciation, essential grammar, and core vocabulary alongside the cultural context that keeps the language alive today. You will learn to read and pronounce Hawaiian words correctly, build simple sentences in Hawaiian's verb-first word order, and use everyday phrases for greetings, family, and counting.
outcomes: You can pronounce all thirteen letters of the Hawaiian alphabet, including the ʻokina and kahakō, and read unfamiliar Hawaiian words aloud correctly.
You can greet someone, ask how they are doing, and respond, entirely in Hawaiian.
You can build a basic Hawaiian sentence using its verb-first (VSO) word order.
You can use ʻo and he correctly to say who or what someone or something is.
You can count from 1 to 10 and name close family members in Hawaiian.
You can explain why the ʻokina and kahakō matter and describe the language's revival since the 1970s.

units.title: Nā Leo — The Sounds of Hawaiian
units.summary: Hawaiian has only thirteen letters, but each one must be pronounced precisely — this unit builds accurate pronunciation from the ground up, including the two marks that change meaning.

lessons.title: The Hawaiian Alphabet and Vowels
lessons.intro: Open any Hawaiian dictionary and you will find only thirteen letters doing all the work — five vowels and eight consonants — yet those thirteen letters can trip up an untrained reader completely, because Hawaiian vowels never bend the way English vowels do.

sections.heading: Five Vowels, Five Sounds
body: Hawaiian has five vowel letters — a, e, i, o, u — and each one keeps exactly one sound, unlike English, where a single letter such as 'a' can sound different in 'cat,' 'father,' and 'about.' Short a sounds like the 'a' in 'above'; short e sounds like the 'e' in 'bet'; short i sounds like the 'ee' in 'see,' only clipped shorter; short o sounds like the 'o' in 'sole'; and short u sounds like the 'oo' in 'moon,' also clipped short.

Because each vowel has only one quality, Hawaiian words are far more predictable to sound out than English ones once you know the five values. The word *aloha* breaks into three vowel-anchored beats, a-lo-ha, and every syllable in Hawaiian ends in a vowel, which is why Hawaiian words so often sound smooth and rolling to an English ear.

example.problem: Sound out the word *mahalo* (thank you) syllable by syllable using the five vowel values above.
steps: Break the word into vowel-anchored syllables: ma-ha-lo.
Pronounce each syllable with its pure vowel: ma ('mah'), ha ('hah'), lo ('loh').
Say the syllables smoothly in sequence without gliding the vowels: ma-ha-lo.
example.answer: mahalo is pronounced mah-HAH-loh, with three clear, even syllables.

sections.heading: Eight Consonants, No Silent Letters
body: Hawaiian uses only eight consonant letters: h, k, l, m, n, p, w, and the ʻokina (treated as a consonant, covered in the next lesson). Six of them — h, k, l, m, n, p — sound almost exactly as they do in English. There are no silent letters in Hawaiian and no consonant clusters like the 'str' in 'string'; every consonant is followed by a vowel, which is why Hawaiian syllables are so consistently open.

The letter w is the one consonant that changes behavior: after u and o it is pronounced like an English 'w' (as in 'wai,' water), but after i and e it is often pronounced like a 'v' (as in 'ʻewa,' pronounced closer to 'EH-vah' by many speakers). After a, either pronunciation is acceptable, and speakers vary by island and family tradition, so both pronunciations of the w in 'Hawaiʻi' are heard in casual speech.

keyTerms.def: A vowel sound that stays constant and does not glide into another sound, as Hawaiian vowels do.
A syllable that ends in a vowel rather than a consonant — the pattern every Hawaiian syllable follows.
The glottal stop, written ʻ, counted as one of Hawaiian's eight consonants.

practice.q: Which best describes how Hawaiian vowels behave compared to English vowels?
choices: Each Hawaiian vowel keeps one pure sound instead of gliding
Hawaiian vowels are pronounced identically to English long vowels
Hawaiian has twice as many vowel sounds as English
practice.explain: English vowels often glide (like the 'a' in 'cake'), but each Hawaiian vowel holds a single, pure quality.

practice.q: How many syllables does 'aloha' have, and how do you know?
choices: Three — a-lo-ha, because every syllable is built around one vowel
One, because it is a single word
Four, because it has four letters that are consonants
Two, because English treats it as two syllables
practice.explain: Hawaiian syllables are vowel-anchored and open, so aloha splits into a-lo-ha: three syllables.

practice.q: After which vowels is the Hawaiian w most often pronounced like an English 'v'?
practice.explain: After i and e, w commonly shifts toward a 'v' sound, as in ʻewa; after u and o it stays a 'w' sound.

lessons.title: The ʻOkina and Kahakō
lessons.intro: Leave out one small mark in Hawaiian and you can turn 'chicken' into 'cooked,' or 'your' into 'my' — the ʻokina and kahakō are not decorations, they are full letters and sounds that carry meaning.

sections.heading: The ʻOkina: A Real Consonant
body: The ʻokina (ʻ) marks a glottal stop, the same brief catch in the throat English speakers make between the two syllables of 'uh-oh.' It is one of Hawaiian's eight consonants, not a punctuation mark, and it must be pronounced — dropping it is a pronunciation error, not a stylistic choice, and it can change a word's entire meaning.

A well-known example is the pair *moa*, a chicken, and *moʻa*, cooked. The children's phrase *E moʻa ka moa* ('Let the chicken be cooked') is often used to teach exactly why the ʻokina cannot be skipped: without it, the sentence would nonsensically say 'let the chicken be a chicken.' The ʻokina also distinguishes *kou* ('your') from *koʻu* ('my'), two words a learner must tell apart correctly to avoid embarrassing mix-ups.

example.problem: Explain the difference in meaning between *kou inoa* and *koʻu inoa*.
steps: *Kou* means 'your' (singular); *koʻu* means 'my.' The only difference in spelling is the ʻokina.
*Inoa* means 'name' in both phrases.
Because the ʻokina is a full consonant, its presence or absence changes the possessor from 'your' to 'my.'
example.answer: *Kou inoa* means 'your name'; *koʻu inoa* means 'my name.'

sections.heading: The Kahakō: Vowel Length That Matters
body: The kahakō is the macron, a short line over a vowel (ā ē ī ō ū) showing that the vowel is held roughly twice as long as its short counterpart and often carries the word's main stress. Words like *kūpuna* (elders, grandparents), *ʻāina* (land), and *kāne* (man) all depend on their macrons for correct pronunciation.

Because macrons are frequently dropped in signage, older texts, and casual typing, learners must memorize which vowels are long in each word rather than relying on what they read around town. A good Hawaiian dictionary always marks both the ʻokina and the kahakō, and building the habit of checking a dictionary early will save you from mispronouncing common words for years.

keyTerms.def: A glottal-stop consonant written ʻ; dropping it can change a word's meaning entirely.
The macron (ā ē ī ō ū) marking a vowel held about twice as long, often with the main stress.
A brief closure of the throat that stops airflow, as in the pause in the English 'uh-oh.'
The line placed over a long vowel; another name for kahakō.

practice.q: What does the ʻokina represent?
practice.explain: The ʻokina is a true consonant, the glottal stop, and must be pronounced.

practice.q: Which pair of words is distinguished only by the ʻokina?
practice.explain: Kou ('your') and koʻu ('my') differ only by the ʻokina, changing the possessor.

practice.q: What does a kahakō (macron) indicate?
choices: The vowel is held about twice as long, often with the main stress
The word is a loanword from English
The syllable is dropped in casual speech
practice.explain: The kahakō lengthens a vowel and typically marks where the word's stress falls.

lessons.title: Syllables and Reading Hawaiian Aloud
lessons.intro: Put the alphabet, the ʻokina, and the kahakō together and you can already sound out almost any Hawaiian word you will ever see on a street sign, a menu, or a song lyric — this lesson is where it all clicks into fluent-sounding reading.

sections.heading: Breaking Words Into Syllables
body: Every Hawaiian syllable is a vowel alone, or a consonant plus a vowel, and syllables never end in a consonant. To read a long word, first mark every vowel, then attach each consonant to the syllable of the vowel that follows it.

Take *Kamehameha*: mark the vowels a-e-a-e-a, then attach each consonant to the vowel after it, giving Ka-me-ha-me-ha, five even syllables. Longer place names such as *Kealakekua* follow the same method — Ke-a-la-ke-kua — and once you can do this mechanically, no Hawaiian word looks intimidating anymore.

sections.heading: Stress and Everyday Practice
body: Stress in Hawaiian usually falls on the second-to-last syllable of a word, unless a macron marks a different syllable as long, in which case the long vowel typically takes the stress instead. In *Ka-me-ha-me-ha*, the stress falls on the second-to-last syllable, *me*, giving Ka-me-HA-me-ha in natural speech.

The best way to build real fluency is to read Hawaiian aloud daily from real sources — place names on a map, song titles, or a phrase book — sounding out every syllable deliberately at first and only speeding up once the pure vowels and consonants feel automatic. Reading slowly and correctly now prevents years of mispronouncing the same words later.

example.problem: Break *Honolulu* into syllables and mark where the stress falls.
steps: Identify the vowels: o-o-u-u, giving four vowel-anchored syllables: Ho-no-lu-lu.
Check for a macron — there is none, so the default stress rule applies.
Apply the default rule: stress falls on the second-to-last syllable, lu.
example.answer: Ho-no-LU-lu, four syllables with stress on the third syllable.

keyTerms.def: A single vowel, or a consonant plus a vowel; Hawaiian syllables never end in a consonant.
In an unmarked word, stress normally falls on the second-to-last syllable.
Two vowel sounds blended within a single syllable, such as the *ai* in *lanai*.

practice.q: How many syllables does *Kamehameha* have?
practice.explain: Each vowel anchors its own syllable, giving five open syllables.

practice.q: Without a macron, where does stress normally fall in a Hawaiian word?
choices: Hawaiian words have no stress pattern
practice.explain: The default Hawaiian stress rule places emphasis on the second-to-last syllable unless a macron says otherwise.

practice.q: Why can a macron override the default stress rule?
choices: A long vowel typically attracts the word's main stress
Macrons are only decorative and never affect stress
Macrons always move stress to the first syllable
Macrons silence the vowel they sit on
practice.explain: A kahakō marks a held, long vowel, which usually pulls the stress onto that syllable.

units.title: E Kipa Mai — Greetings and Everyday Phrases
units.summary: Aloha is only the beginning — this unit builds a full toolkit of greetings, introductions, and the small polite words that carry a conversation.

lessons.title: Aloha: Greetings and Farewells
lessons.intro: Aloha is the first Hawaiian word most visitors learn and the last one many think about fully — it means hello, goodbye, and love all at once, and this lesson gives you a full set of greetings to go with it.

sections.heading: Hello and Goodbye
body: *Aloha* works as both 'hello' and 'goodbye,' so context tells a listener which one you mean — said on arrival it welcomes, said on departure it sends off. For a time-specific greeting, Hawaiian adds a word for the part of day: *aloha kakahiaka* (good morning), *aloha ʻauinalā* (good afternoon), and *aloha ahiahi* (good evening).

*Aloha* is also used as a warm way to address a letter or a crowd, similar to 'dear' or 'everyone.' A simple, correct greeting to open any conversation is *Aloha kāua*, literally 'aloha to the two of us,' a friendly way to greet one other person directly.

sections.heading: Introducing Yourself
body: To introduce yourself, say *ʻO [name] koʻu inoa* — literally '[Name] is my name.' For example, *ʻO Kimo koʻu inoa* means 'My name is Kimo.' To ask someone's name in return, say *ʻO wai kou inoa?* ('What is your name?'), using the question word *wai* ('who').

To say goodbye when you expect to see someone again soon, Hawaiian uses *A hui hou*, literally 'until we meet again,' which is warmer and more specific than a plain *aloha*. Pairing *Aloha* with *A hui hou* at the end of a conversation is common and natural.

example.problem: Introduce yourself as 'Malia' in Hawaiian, then say goodbye expecting to meet again.
steps: Use the pattern ʻO [name] koʻu inoa for introducing yourself.
Insert 'Malia': ʻO Malia koʻu inoa.
Close with the goodbye phrase for 'see you again': A hui hou.
example.answer: ʻO Malia koʻu inoa. A hui hou.

keyTerms.def: A greeting meaning hello, goodbye, and love, understood from context.
'Until we meet again' — a warm goodbye used when you expect to see someone soon.
'What is your name?' — literally asking who your name is.

practice.q: What determines whether *aloha* means 'hello' or 'goodbye'?
choices: Context — the situation it is said in
A different spelling is used for each
practice.explain: Aloha is one word covering both greetings and farewells; context tells you which is meant.

practice.q: Which phrase correctly introduces yourself as 'Kimo'?
practice.explain: The pattern ʻO [name] koʻu inoa literally states '[Name] is my name.'

practice.q: What does *A hui hou* mean, and when is it used?
choices: 'Until we meet again,' used when you expect to see someone soon
practice.explain: A hui hou is a specific goodbye meaning you expect a future meeting, warmer than a bare aloha.

lessons.title: Pehea ʻOe? Asking How Someone Is
lessons.intro: Once you can say hello, the next thing any conversation needs is a way to ask how someone is doing and to answer honestly — Hawaiian gives you the tools in just a few short phrases.

sections.heading: Asking the Question
body: *Pehea ʻoe?* means 'How are you?', built from *pehea* ('how') and *ʻoe* ('you,' singular). To ask about more than one person, swap in *ʻoukou* ('you all'): *Pehea ʻoukou?* To ask how a third person is doing, use *ʻo ia* ('he/she'): *Pehea ʻo ia?*

Hawaiian question words go where English speakers might expect an answer to go, at the front: *pehea* (how), *ʻo wai* (who — for names), *aha* (what), and *hea* (where/which) all typically open the question, similar to English 'wh-' words.

sections.heading: Answering How You Are
body: The most common good answer is *Maikaʻi au* ('I am fine/good'), sometimes strengthened to *Maikaʻi loa au* ('I am very good'). If you are not feeling well, *ʻAʻole maikaʻi* means 'not good.' To return the question, add *A ʻo ʻoe?* ('And you?') after your answer.

A full exchange might run: *Pehea ʻoe?* — *Maikaʻi au, mahalo. A ʻo ʻoe?* — *Maikaʻi nō hoʻi au* ('I'm doing well too'). Notice *mahalo* ('thank you') slots in naturally right after the answer, just as 'thanks' would in English.

example.problem: Write a short exchange: ask 'How are you?', answer 'I am very good, thank you,' then ask the question back.
steps: Ask: Pehea ʻoe?
Answer with intensifier and thanks: Maikaʻi loa au, mahalo.
Return the question: A ʻo ʻoe?
example.answer: Pehea ʻoe? — Maikaʻi loa au, mahalo. A ʻo ʻoe?

keyTerms.def: 'How are you?' — pehea means 'how,' ʻoe means 'you' (singular).
Good, fine, well — the standard positive answer to 'how are you.'
'He/she' — used to ask or talk about a third person.

practice.q: What does *Pehea ʻoe?* literally ask?
practice.explain: Pehea means 'how' and ʻoe means 'you' (one person), so it literally asks how you are.

practice.q: Which word would you swap in to ask a group 'how are you all'?
practice.explain: ʻOukou means 'you all,' replacing the singular ʻoe to address a group.

practice.q: How would you say 'I am very good, thank you'?
practice.explain: Loa intensifies maikaʻi to 'very good,' and mahalo adds 'thank you.'

lessons.title: Please, Thank You, Yes, and No
lessons.intro: A handful of small words carry enormous social weight in any language, and Hawaiian's words for thanks, yes, and no are used constantly in daily life on the islands, in emails, and in casual speech alike.

sections.heading: Mahalo and Politeness
body: *Mahalo* means 'thank you,' and *mahalo nui loa* strengthens it to 'thank you very much.' Hawaiian does not have a single dedicated word for 'please' the way English does; politeness is instead carried by softer phrasing, adding *e ʻoluʻolu* ('if you would be so kind') before a request, roughly matching the function of 'please.'

*E kala mai* means 'excuse me' or 'I'm sorry,' useful both for interrupting politely and for apologizing for a small mistake. Combining these, a polite request might sound like *E ʻoluʻolu, e kōkua mai* ('Please, help me'), where *kōkua* means 'to help.'

example.problem: Politely ask someone to help you, then thank them.
steps: Open with the please-equivalent phrase: E ʻoluʻolu.
Add the request using kōkua (help): e kōkua mai.
Close with thanks: Mahalo.
example.answer: E ʻoluʻolu, e kōkua mai. Mahalo.

sections.heading: Yes and No
body: *ʻAe* means 'yes,' and *ʻaʻole* means 'no.' Both can stand alone as a full answer, just like English 'yes' and 'no.' *ʻAʻole* also attaches to a verb to negate it, similar to 'not' in English — *ʻAʻole au makemake* means 'I do not want (that).'

Listen for the difference in length: *ʻae* is short and crisp, while *ʻaʻole* has an extra syllable and an ʻokina in the middle, ʻa-ʻo-le. Mixing these up is a common beginner mistake, so practicing them side by side out loud is worth the extra minute.

keyTerms.def: Thank you; mahalo nui loa means 'thank you very much.'
Yes / no — ʻaʻole can also negate a verb, like 'not.'
A softening phrase used where English would say 'please.'

practice.q: What does *mahalo nui loa* mean?
practice.explain: Nui loa intensifies mahalo ('thank you') to 'very much.'

practice.q: How does Hawaiian typically express 'please'?
choices: With softening phrases like e ʻoluʻolu rather than one dedicated word
With the word mahalo repeated twice
There is no way to be polite in Hawaiian
practice.explain: Hawaiian carries politeness through phrasing such as e ʻoluʻolu rather than a single equivalent of 'please.'

practice.q: What is the key difference between ʻae and ʻaʻole?
choices: ʻAe means yes; ʻaʻole means no and can also negate a verb
They are two ways to say the same word, yes
ʻAe is formal, ʻaʻole is a nickname
ʻAʻole is only used with children
practice.explain: ʻAe is 'yes'; ʻaʻole is 'no' and doubles as a negator attached to verbs.

units.title: Ke Kūkulu ʻŌlelo — Building Sentences
units.summary: Hawaiian grammar reorders and reclassifies in ways English does not — this unit covers verb-first word order, saying what something is, and the two classes of possession.

lessons.title: Verb-First Word Order
lessons.intro: In English the subject always comes first — 'I run,' 'She sings' — but Hawaiian puts the action first, and getting comfortable with that reversal is the single biggest shift in thinking a new Hawaiian learner has to make.

sections.heading: VSO: Verb, Subject, Object
body: Hawaiian sentences typically follow Verb-Subject-Object order, the reverse of English's Subject-Verb-Object. *Holoholo au* means 'I am cruising around' — literally 'cruising-around I' — with the verb *holoholo* first and the subject *au* ('I') second. When an object is added it comes last: *ʻAi au i ka poi* ('I eat the poi'), literally 'eat I [object marker] the poi.'

The small word *i* (or *iā* before a person's name) marks the object. Without *i*, a listener could not easily tell where the subject ends and the object begins, since Hawaiian nouns do not change form to show their role in the sentence the way English pronouns like 'he/him' do.

sections.heading: Present-Tense Markers
body: Because Hawaiian verbs do not conjugate by adding endings the way English verbs do ('walk' → 'walks'), tense and aspect are shown by short marker words placed before the verb. *Ke* ... *nei* wraps around the verb to show an action happening right now: *Ke ʻai nei au* means 'I am eating (right now).'

Without the *ke*...*nei* frame, a bare verb sentence like *ʻAi au* often reads as a general or habitual statement, closer to 'I eat.' Learning to add or drop this frame is how a Hawaiian speaker signals whether something is happening this instant or generally true.

example.problem: Translate 'I am drinking water' into Hawaiian, using *inu* (to drink) and *wai* (water), marking that it is happening right now.
steps: Start with the verb frame for present action: Ke ... nei.
Insert the verb inu: Ke inu nei.
Add the subject au ('I'): Ke inu nei au.
Add the object marker i and the object wai: Ke inu nei au i ka wai.
example.answer: Ke inu nei au i ka wai. ('I am drinking the water.')

keyTerms.def: Verb-Subject-Object, Hawaiian's basic sentence order, opposite of English's Subject-Verb-Object.
A word placed before a direct object; iā is used before a person's name.
A verb frame marking an action happening right now, roughly '-ing' in English.

practice.q: What is Hawaiian's basic sentence word order?
choices: Hawaiian has no fixed word order
practice.explain: Hawaiian places the verb first, then the subject, then any object — VSO order.

practice.q: In *ʻAi au i ka poi*, what role does *i* play?
choices: It marks ka poi as the object of the verb
practice.explain: i (here i ka, 'the') introduces the direct object, showing what is being eaten.

practice.q: What does the frame *ke ... nei* around a verb indicate?
choices: The action is happening right now
The action happened in the distant past
practice.explain: Ke...nei marks present, ongoing action, similar to English '-ing.'

lessons.title: Saying What Something Is: He and ʻO
lessons.intro: Hawaiian has no verb 'to be' the way English does — there is no word for 'is' or 'am' — so identifying who or what something is relies entirely on two small marker words, *he* and *ʻo*, and knowing which one to use.

sections.heading: He: A or An
body: *He* introduces an indefinite noun, roughly matching English 'a' or 'an,' and it opens a sentence that classifies something: *He kumu ʻo Kimo* means 'Kimo is a teacher,' literally 'a teacher [is] Kimo.' The sentence order here is Predicate-Subject, another reversal from English, where the class or description comes first and the named person comes second.

*He* sentences describe a category, quantity, or general description rather than pointing at one specific, already-known thing: *He hale nui kēia* means 'This is a big house.' If you are describing what kind of thing something is, *he* is almost always the right choice to open the sentence.

sections.heading: ʻO: Naming a Specific Person or Thing
body: *ʻO* introduces a specific, already-identified person, place, or thing being named or pointed out, and it is required before proper names in many sentence patterns: *ʻO Maui kēia* means 'This is Maui.' Where *he* classifies, *ʻo* identifies — it answers 'which one,' not 'what kind.'

You already used *ʻo* to introduce yourself in Unit 2: *ʻO Kimo koʻu inoa* ('Kimo is my name') names a specific name, not a category of name. Mixing up *he* and *ʻo* is one of the most common beginner errors, so a useful check is to ask whether you are naming a specific thing (*ʻo*) or classifying it (*he*).

example.problem: Say 'This is a big island' (classifying, using *he* and *moku* for island) versus 'This is Kauaʻi' (naming a specific island).
steps: For the classifying sentence, open with he: He moku nui kēia.
For naming a specific island, open with ʻo and the proper name: ʻO Kauaʻi kēia.
example.answer: He moku nui kēia. ('This is a big island.') / ʻO Kauaʻi kēia. ('This is Kauaʻi.')

keyTerms.def: A marker introducing an indefinite, classifying noun, roughly 'a/an.'
A marker introducing a specific, named person or thing; required before many proper names.
The pattern in he/ʻo sentences where the description or name comes before the thing it describes.

practice.q: Which marker would you use to say 'This is a big house' (classifying, not naming)?
practice.explain: He introduces a classifying, indefinite description like 'a big house.'

practice.q: Which marker is required to introduce a specific name, as in 'This is Maui'?
practice.explain: ʻO introduces a specific, identified name or thing, unlike the classifying he.

practice.q: What question does *ʻo* answer, as opposed to *he*?
choices: They are interchangeable in every context
practice.explain: ʻO identifies a specific individual thing, while he classifies what kind of thing something is.

lessons.title: Possession: Kāʻu and Koʻu, the A and O Classes
lessons.intro: Hawaiian possession is not one-size-fits-all: whether you say 'my dog' or 'my father' uses a completely different set of words, because Hawaiian sorts possessions into two classes based on how much control you have over them.

sections.heading: The A-Class: Things You Control
body: The a-class covers possessions you acquire, produce, or control — spouses, children, food, drinks, tools, and things you do to others. Its possessive words include *kāʻu* (my), *kāu* (your), and *kāna* (his/her), all built on *a*. *Kāʻu keiki* means 'my child,' because in Hawaiian thought a parent is understood as bringing a child into being.

Food and drink are almost always a-class because you choose and prepare them: *kāʻu iʻa* ('my fish,' meaning fish you caught or are about to eat) uses the a-class possessive. The underlying logic is agency: if you brought the thing about or actively control it, use the a-form.

sections.heading: The O-Class: Things That Possess You
body: The o-class covers things you did not choose or cannot control — parents, body parts, land, houses, clothing you wear, feelings, and vehicles or spaces that contain you. Its possessive words include *koʻu* (my), *kou* (your), and *kona* (his/her), all built on *o*. *Koʻu makuahine* means 'my mother,' because you do not choose or control your parent.

The logic flips for things like a house or a canoe: even though you might own a house, Hawaiian treats it as o-class because the house contains and shelters you, rather than you controlling it the way you control a tool. *Koʻu hale* ('my house') and *koʻu lima* ('my hand,' a body part) both follow this inherent, uncontrolled-relationship pattern.

example.problem: Choose the correct possessive for 'my father' and 'my dog,' explaining the class of each.
steps: 'Father' (makua kāne) is a parent, uncontrolled and inherent, so it takes the o-class: koʻu makua kāne.
'Dog' (ʻīlio) is typically treated as something acquired and cared for by the owner, so it takes the a-class: kāʻu ʻīlio.
example.answer: koʻu makua kāne ('my father,' o-class) and kāʻu ʻīlio ('my dog,' a-class).

keyTerms.def: Possessives (kāʻu, kāu, kāna) for things acquired, produced, or controlled, like food, tools, and children.
Possessives (koʻu, kou, kona) for things inherent or uncontrolled, like parents, body parts, and houses.
The idea of control or having brought something about, which decides whether a possession is a-class or o-class.

practice.q: Which class does 'my mother' (koʻu makuahine) belong to, and why?
choices: O-class, because a parent is not something you control or choose
A-class, because it is a formal relationship
practice.explain: Parents are inherent, uncontrolled relationships, so Hawaiian marks them with o-class possessives.

practice.q: Why is 'my house' (koʻu hale) o-class rather than a-class, even though you own it?
choices: The house contains and shelters you rather than you controlling it like a tool
Houses are always free in Hawaiian culture
Ownership is irrelevant to Hawaiian grammar
Hale is a loanword and follows English rules
practice.explain: O-class covers things that contain or are inherent to you, like a house or a body part, not just legal ownership.

practice.q: Which possessive correctly means 'my child' (a-class)?
practice.explain: Children are a-class because a parent is understood to bring the child into being; kāʻu is the a-class 'my.'

units.title: ʻOhana, Helu, a me ka Moʻomeheu — Family, Numbers, and Culture
units.summary: The final unit fills out your Hawaiian toolkit with family vocabulary, counting, and the story of how the language nearly disappeared and came back.

lessons.title: Family Words: ʻOhana
lessons.intro: *ʻOhana* means far more than 'family' in the narrow sense — it names a whole network of relationships and obligations — but before exploring that idea, you need the basic vocabulary for the people inside it.

sections.heading: Parents, Siblings, and Children
body: *Makuahine* means mother, *makua kāne* means father, and together *mau mākua* means parents. *Keiki* means child, and *kaikamahine* and *keikikāne* specify daughter and son. Siblings are labeled by relative age and by the speaker's gender: *kaikuaʻana* is an older sibling of the same gender as the speaker, and *kaikaina* is a younger one of the same gender.

Cross-gender sibling terms work differently: *kaikunāne* is a woman's brother, and *kaikuahine* is a man's sister. This means the same person can be called by two different words depending on who is speaking — a man calls his sister *kaikuahine*, but she calls him *kaikunāne*.

sections.heading: Grandparents and the Wider ʻOhana
body: *Kupuna* means an elder or grandparent (plural *kūpuna*, note the long ū), and *moʻopuna* means grandchild. *ʻOhana* itself comes from *ʻohā*, the young shoot that grows from the root of the kalo (taro) plant — the family is imagined as one root system feeding many shoots, which is why the word carries such a strong sense of connectedness.

In practice, *ʻohana* extends well past the biological household: close friends, mentors, and community members are often called *ʻohana* too, reflecting a broader cultural value of *aloha* and mutual care beyond blood relation. Understanding this helps explain why the phrase '*ʻohana* means nobody gets left behind' is used even outside Hawaiʻi.

example.problem: A woman is describing her older brother. Which word does she use, and would her brother use the same word for her?
steps: Because she is a woman referring to her brother, she uses kaikunāne.
Her brother, referring to her (his sister), would use a different word: kaikuahine.
The words are gender-linked to the speaker, not to age alone.
example.answer: She says kaikunāne; he would call her kaikuahine — the terms depend on the speaker's own gender.

keyTerms.def: Family, in a broad sense including extended relatives and close non-blood relations.
Elder, grandparent (singular/plural) — a respected older family or community member.
Older sibling / younger sibling of the same gender as the speaker.
A woman's brother / a man's sister — cross-gender sibling terms.

practice.q: What does *kupuna* (plural *kūpuna*) mean?
practice.explain: Kupuna refers to an elder or grandparent, a respected older generation.

practice.q: If a man is talking about his sister, which word does he use?
practice.explain: Kaikuahine is specifically a man's word for his sister; her word for him would be kaikunāne.

practice.q: Why does ʻohana carry a broader meaning than the English word 'family'?
choices: It derives from the taro plant's root system and extends to close non-blood relations
It only refers to parents and children, nothing else
It is a recent English loanword
It refers only to ancestors who have passed away
practice.explain: ʻOhana comes from ʻohā, the shoots of the kalo plant, symbolizing a shared root that extends to close friends and community, not just blood relatives.

lessons.title: Counting: Nā Helu ʻEkahi a ʻUmi
lessons.intro: Numbers show up everywhere — prices, addresses, ages, phone numbers — and Hawaiian's counting words follow a clean, learnable pattern built almost entirely on the prefix *ʻe-*.

sections.heading: One Through Ten
body: The numbers one through nine are built with the prefix *ʻe-* plus a root: *ʻekahi* (1), *ʻelua* (2), *ʻekolu* (3), *ʻehā* (4), *ʻelima* (5), *ʻeono* (6), *ʻehiku* (7), *ʻewalu* (8), and *ʻeiwa* (9). Ten breaks the pattern with its own word, *ʻumi*, which does not take the *ʻe-* prefix.

Notice the roots recur in later numbers too: *lua* (two) reappears in *ʻiwakālua* (twenty), and *kolu* (three) reappears in *kanakolu* (thirty). Learning the one-through-nine roots solidly now pays off directly when you move on to bigger numbers, because Hawaiian builds them compositionally rather than inventing a new word for every ten.

sections.heading: Counting Things, Not Just Numbers
body: When counting actual objects rather than reciting numbers in a list, Hawaiian typically adds *ʻo* before the number: *ʻehia keiki?* asks 'how many children?' and an answer like *ʻekolu* becomes *ʻo ʻekolu* ('three [of them]') in that counting context. This *ʻo* is the same marker introduced earlier for identifying specific things, now applied to specify a specific count.

Ages also use numbers directly: *ʻehia ona makahiki?* asks how many years someone is (how old they are), and the answer follows the pattern number + *makahiki* (years), such as *ʻumi makahiki* ('ten years old'). Practicing counting objects around you — fingers, chairs, steps — is the fastest way to make these numbers automatic.

example.problem: Someone asks *ʻEhia keiki?* (How many children?) and the answer is five. Give the full answer.
steps: Recall the number five: ʻelima.
In a counting-things context, prefix with ʻo: ʻo ʻelima.
State the full answer: ʻO ʻelima. ('Five.')

keyTerms.def: The prefix attached to the roots of numbers one through nine (ʻekahi, ʻelua, ...).
Ten — the one number one-through-ten that does not take the ʻe- prefix.
'How many?' — the question word used to ask for a count.

practice.q: Which number does NOT take the ʻe- prefix?
practice.explain: ʻUmi (ten) has its own root and does not follow the ʻe- + root pattern of one through nine.

practice.q: What does *ʻehia* mean?
practice.explain: ʻEhia is the question word used to ask for a count of things.

practice.q: How would you say 'three' in answer to a counting question like ʻEhia keiki?
practice.explain: ʻO plus the number (ʻekolu, three) is the standard way to answer a counting question.

lessons.title: A Living Language: Revival and Renaissance
lessons.intro: For most of the 20th century it looked possible that ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi would disappear entirely — by the early 1980s only a few dozen native child speakers remained — yet today Hawaiian is taught in preschools, spoken at home, and required study in this course; understanding how that happened is part of learning the language itself.

sections.heading: Suppression and Near Loss
body: After the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom in 1893 and annexation by the United States, a law passed in 1896 mandated English as the sole language of instruction in schools, and children who spoke Hawaiian at school were commonly punished. Over the following decades, the number of fluent speakers dropped sharply, concentrated increasingly among older generations and the small, isolated community on the island of Niʻihau.

By the early 1980s, researchers estimated that fewer than fifty children under age eighteen spoke Hawaiian fluently outside Niʻihau, placing the language at serious risk of dying out within a generation. This crisis point is exactly what galvanized the recovery effort that followed.

sections.heading: The Hawaiian Renaissance and Revival
body: Hawaiian became an official state language alongside English at the 1978 Hawaiʻi State Constitutional Convention, part of a broader cultural resurgence known as the Hawaiian Renaissance that also revived voyaging canoes, hula traditions, and Hawaiian music. In 1983, a group of educators and parents founded ʻAha Pūnana Leo, and the first Hawaiian-language immersion preschool opened the following year, giving young children a place to grow up speaking Hawaiian as a first language again.

That preschool model grew into full immersion programs through high school, called Kula Kaiapuni, and Hawaiian is now taught at every level from preschool through university, including Hawaiian-medium degree programs. The number of Hawaiian speakers has grown substantially since the 1980s low point, though the language remains classified as endangered, and its continued strength depends directly on new learners like you choosing to study and use it.

example.problem: Explain in one or two sentences why the founding of ʻAha Pūnana Leo in 1983 was a turning point for the Hawaiian language.
steps: Before 1983, Hawaiian had almost no children learning it as a first language, putting it on a path toward extinction within a generation.
ʻAha Pūnana Leo created immersion preschools starting in 1984, giving children an environment to acquire Hawaiian natively again.
This restarted intergenerational transmission of the language, the key ingredient for a language's survival.
example.answer: It restarted natural, child-to-child transmission of Hawaiian at a moment when almost no children were learning it, reversing a trend toward extinction.

keyTerms.def: A cultural resurgence from the 1970s onward reviving Hawaiian language, voyaging, hula, and music.
The organization founded in 1983 that opened the first Hawaiian-language immersion preschools.
Hawaiian-language immersion schools that extend the Pūnana Leo model through K-12 education.
A language at risk of falling out of use because it is not being learned by enough new speakers.

practice.q: What 1896 law severely damaged the Hawaiian language?
choices: A law mandating English as the sole language of school instruction
A ban on speaking Hawaiian in private homes
A requirement that all books be written only in Hawaiian
practice.explain: The 1896 law made English the only language of instruction, and speaking Hawaiian at school was commonly punished afterward.

practice.q: What did ʻAha Pūnana Leo establish starting in 1984?
choices: A ban on English in government
practice.explain: ʻAha Pūnana Leo opened the first Hawaiian immersion preschool in 1984, restarting child acquisition of the language.

practice.q: Why was the small population of fluent child speakers in the early 1980s considered a crisis?
choices: Without children learning the language, it faced dying out within a generation
It meant Hawaiian had officially become extinct already
It showed that adults had stopped understanding Hawaiian entirely
It meant the language had never been written down
practice.explain: A language survives only if children learn it; with so few young fluent speakers, Hawaiian was on the edge of losing intergenerational transmission.
